pr_title: sql/catalog: address session based leasing bugs
pr_body:
This patch addresses the following issues:
1. Previously the session based leasing upgrade had a race condition against the leasing count queries, which could cause them to incorrect expect the wrong version of the descriptor. To address this, we are going to start using the system database descriptor version to determine if synthetic descriptors should be used (instead of cluster settings).
2. The repair_schema logictest had an intermittent failure because it was force deleting and injecting descriptors instantly. This runs into an existing design limitation of the lease manager where deleted descriptors are instantly cleaned up from memory, but asynchronously removed from storage. When we inject the descriptor with the exact same versions, the lease manager would detect a duplicate row and fails renewing (in the session based model). This condition can only be hit by repair queries and in the expiry based model would lead to duplicate rows. For the purpose of testing we are going to intentionally give a new version when adding the descriptor back, since the sequence in general dangerous with repair queries (i.e. e need to confirm that the lease is no longer in use before injecting the descriptor again or set a new version).


Fixes: #120445 
Fixes #120735 
Fixes #120675

comments:
The errors are coming from DROP TABLE, and the raw_bytes are encoded as a mixed of octal and ASCII:
       ``` (XXUUU) unexpected value: raw_bytes:"\321\376\216\236\n3\002" timestamp:<wall_time:1710864440363971470 > ```
I'm still trying to figure out where this value is being surfaced.

None of the tricks I tried to decode it worked. is there a different way?
```
root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> select e'\257\237s\312\n3\002'::bytea;
ERROR: statement ignored: lexical error: invalid UTF-8 byte sequence
SQLSTATE: 42601
DETAIL: source SQL:
select e'\257\237s\312\n3\002'::bytea;
       ^
root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> select decode(e'\257\237s\312\n3\002', 'escape');
ERROR: statement ignored: lexical error: invalid UTF-8 byte sequence
SQLSTATE: 42601
DETAIL: source SQL:
select decode(e'\257\237s\312\n3\002', 'escape');
              ^
HINT: try \hf decode
root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> select decode('\257\237s\312\n3\002', 'escape');
ERROR: decode(): invalid bytea escape sequence
SQLSTATE: 22025
```

Because its a mix I hand decoded the octals and the ASCII characters so its pretty painful :(. The example above has ASCII 's', '\n', '3' as normal characters, and everything else is an octal (no clue why the protobuf formatter is like that for byte arrays).
Ah wow. So in hex, the `raw_bytes:"\257\237s\312\n3\002"` value is `af9f73ca0a3302`. I think the round-trippable way to print that would be `\257\237s\312\0123\002`.

Oh never-mind its the SELECT that hits the error. But the error is coming from the acquireNodeLease code path when the lease manager attempts to acquire it and sees and existing row. I think there is a race condition against the repair functions.

So adding more detail here this happens because crdb_internal.force_delete_table_data does not wait for descriptor leases to disappear. Afterwards, we ingest the descriptor with the *exact* same ID / version again. The lease clean up process for deletion is asynchronous when deleting the row from the system.lease table, so while that is on going we can have have a race condition with an acquisition on the *exact* same descriptor and version. (which happens on the SELECT). The acquisition expects no row since we cleaned it up from memory but **not** storage.

The scenario we are seeing can only be hit with repair functions, since descriptors don't normally come back from the dead. i.e. Asynchronous deletion at the storage layer for leasing is safe under normal scenarios. 

For the purpose of this test, I'm going to modify the repair query to bump the version number on the ingested descriptor. We could do something more complex at the leasing layer for the deletion to block renewals if the descriptors comes back from the dead, however its not worth the complexity and risk (i.e. delete the in memory entry after the storage layer cleans up).

One more question: once we have the byte value `\257\237s\312\0123\002`, then how do we know what key that corresponds to? this didn't seem to work:
```
root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> select crdb_internal.pretty_key('\257\237s\312\0123\002'::bytea, 0);
  crdb_internal.pretty_key
----------------------------
  /39/23/"s\xca\n3\x02"
```
@rafiss Its actually a value not a key, and its the node id. It corresponds to the only value stored in the leasing table (session based).
